meta.title: Process costing: the weighted-average method
meta.summary: When process costing applies, equivalent units, the five-step approach, weighted-average physical and equivalent units, cost per equivalent unit and assigning costs, and journal entries between departments.

videos.title: Process costing basics
videos.take: Process costing averages a department's costs over the identical units it produces

scenes.say: When every unit is identical, you don't need a job record for each one. You average. That's process costing.

sub: Cheddar cheese blocks, made in Marshall:
scenes.say: Meet Redwood Valley Creamery, a Marshall cheese maker. Milk goes through two departments: Mixing, where it's cultured, curdled and pressed into blocks, and Aging, where blocks mature before sale. Every block is the same, so it uses process costing.

scenes.heading: Job vs process
scenes.say: Job costing collects costs by job. Process costing collects them by department for a period, then divides by the units produced. Each department has its own work-in-process account.

scenes.heading: February: no beginning or ending WIP
scenes.say: In the simplest case, all work started in the month is finished. In February, Mixing spent $540,000 on milk and cultures and $324,000 on conversion costs, and finished eighteen thousand blocks: forty-eight dollars a block.
The complication comes when some blocks are only partly finished at the end of the month. That's where equivalent units come in.

scenes.q: Costs $250,000; 10,000 units started and completed; no WIP. Cost per unit?
scenes.say: Quick check. Costs two hundred fifty thousand; ten thousand units started and completed; no work in process. Cost per unit? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Equivalent units
videos.take: Equivalent units convert partly finished units into the number of whole units that work would make

scenes.say: Four thousand blocks are only a quarter done. How many finished blocks is that worth? Equivalent units answer that.
Equivalent units are the number of complete units that could have been made with the work actually done. Multiply physical units by their percentage of completion, separately for each cost category.

scenes.heading: 4,000 blocks in ending WIP
scenes.say: In Mixing, all the milk is added at the start, so four thousand blocks in process are a hundred percent complete for materials: four thousand equivalent units. But they're only twenty-five percent through conversion: a thousand equivalent units.

sub: Materials often go in at a point;
scenes.say: That's why we compute equivalent units separately. Materials are often added at a particular point, while conversion costs are incurred evenly through the process.

Who decides a block is twenty-five percent complete? Supervisors estimate it, helped by process timings and sensors. The estimates matter, because they split costs between finished and unfinished units.

scenes.q: 2,000 units are 60% complete for conversion. Conversion equivalent units?
scenes.say: Quick check. Two thousand units are sixty percent complete for conversion. How many conversion equivalent units? Pause and pick.

videos.title: The five-step approach
videos.take: Summarize physical units, compute equivalent units, total the costs, compute cost per EU, assign costs

scenes.say: Every process costing problem follows the same five steps. Learn them, and the method doesn't matter.

scenes.heading: Five steps
items: Summarize total costs to account for
Assign costs to units out and in WIP
scenes.say: Step one: summarize the flow of physical units. Step two: compute equivalent units for each cost category. Step three: summarize the total costs to account for. Step four: compute the cost per equivalent unit. Step five: assign costs to units completed and to ending work in process.

scenes.heading: Mixing, March: the data
scenes.say: Here's Mixing in March. It began with two thousand blocks, forty percent converted, carrying $56,000 of materials and $16,000 of conversion cost. It started eighteen thousand blocks, finished sixteen thousand and ended with four thousand, a quarter converted. March added $540,000 of materials and $324,000 of conversion cost.

scenes.heading: Two methods
scenes.say: There are two methods. Weighted average blends the work done last month on beginning inventory with this month's work. FIFO keeps them separate. This lecture covers weighted average; Lecture 9 covers FIFO.

sub: So every block in Mixing is 100%
scenes.say: One fact to remember for Mixing: all materials go in at the start, so every block in process is complete for materials.

scenes.q: Which step comes after computing equivalent units?
opts: Summarize total costs to account for
scenes.say: Quick check. Which step comes after computing equivalent units? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B: summarize the total costs to account for.

videos.title: Weighted average: units
videos.take: Weighted-average equivalent units = units completed + equivalent units in ending WIP

scenes.say: Steps one and two under weighted average. The rule is simple: completed units, plus the equivalent units still in process.

scenes.heading: Step 1: physical units
scenes.say: Step one. Two thousand blocks in beginning inventory plus eighteen thousand started gives twenty thousand to account for. Sixteen thousand were completed and four thousand remain in process: twenty thousand accounted for.

Weighted-average equivalent units are units completed, which are a hundred percent done, plus the equivalent units in ending work in process. It doesn't matter whether the completed units started this month or last.

scenes.heading: Step 2: equivalent units
scenes.say: For materials: sixteen thousand completed plus four thousand in ending inventory, twenty thousand equivalent units. For conversion: sixteen thousand plus a quarter of four thousand, seventeen thousand.

sub: Under weighted average, its earlier work
scenes.say: Notice that the forty percent completion of beginning inventory never entered the calculation. Weighted average treats last month's work as if it were done this month.

scenes.q: Completed 9,000 units; ending WIP 1,500 units, 40% converted. WA conversion equivalent units?
scenes.say: Quick check. Nine thousand units completed; fifteen hundred in ending inventory, forty percent converted. Weighted-average conversion equivalent units? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Nine thousand plus six hundred is ninety-six hundred.

videos.title: Weighted average: costs
videos.take: WA cost per EU = (beginning WIP cost + current cost) ÷ WA equivalent units

scenes.say: Steps three to five. Add up the costs, divide by equivalent units, and assign.

scenes.heading: Steps 3 and 4: cost per equivalent unit
scenes.say: Materials: $56,000 in beginning inventory plus $540,000 added, $596,000, divided by twenty thousand equivalent units: $29.80. Conversion: $16,000 plus $324,000, $340,000, divided by seventeen thousand: twenty dollars.

scenes.heading: Step 5: assign costs
scenes.say: Each completed block costs $49.80: sixteen thousand of them is $796,800, transferred to Aging. Ending inventory gets four thousand materials units at $29.80 and a thousand conversion units at twenty dollars: $139,200. Together, $936,000, exactly the costs to account for.
Always check: the costs assigned must equal the total costs to account for, here $936,000.
Weighted average is simple, but it blends last month's costs with this month's, which can blur changes in efficiency or prices.

scenes.q: Total conversion costs $90,000; WA conversion EU 18,000. Cost per EU?
scenes.say: Quick check. Total conversion costs ninety thousand; weighted-average conversion equivalent units eighteen thousand. Cost per equivalent unit? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Journal entries in process costing
videos.take: Each department has its own WIP account; completed units transfer cost to the next department

scenes.say: In process costing, costs move from department to department, each with its own work-in-process account.

scenes.heading: Costs added in Mixing, March
scenes.say: Materials put into Mixing debit work in process Mixing and credit materials: $540,000. Conversion costs, labor and applied overhead, debit work in process Mixing for $324,000.

scenes.heading: Transfer to Aging
scenes.say: Completed blocks move to Aging. Debit work in process Aging, credit work in process Mixing: $796,800. In Aging, these become transferred-in costs.

scenes.heading: WIP: Mixing, March
scenes.say: The Mixing T-account: $72,000 beginning balance, plus $540,000 and $324,000 added, less $796,800 transferred out, leaves $139,200, the ending inventory we computed.

sub: when blocks are ready to sell
scenes.say: Aging adds its own conversion costs, then transfers finished blocks to finished goods. That's Lecture 9.

scenes.q: Which entry moves completed blocks from Mixing to Aging?
opts: Dr WIP Mixing, Cr WIP Aging
Dr WIP Aging, Cr WIP Mixing
Dr Finished goods, Cr WIP Mixing
scenes.say: Quick check. Which entry moves completed blocks from Mixing to Aging? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Debit Aging, credit Mixing.

warmup: A bakery mixes 1,000 loaves of dough, and at 5 p.m. 200 are still rising. How many 'loaves' of baking work did the bakers do?
Not 1,000 or 800: the 200 are part-done. Introduces equivalent units.
acts: Job or process costing, and why: a cheese maker, a dairy that also makes custom cheese gift boxes for corporate orders.
Cheese: process. Gift boxes: job costing for the boxes (or a hybrid).
Ending WIP 3,000 units: materials 100%, conversion 70%. Compute EU for each.

Physical units 20,000; EU 20,000 / 17,000; costs 936,000; cost per EU 29.80 / 20.00; assignment 796,800 / 139,200.
April: beginning WIP 4,000 (25% converted; DM $119,200, CC $20,000); started 17,000; completed 18,000; ending 3,000 (60% converted). DM added $516,000; CC $354,000. Compute WA EU.
Continue April: costs per EU and assignment.
Write the journal entries for April's costs and transfer.
Dr WIP Mixing 516,000 / Cr Materials 516,000; Dr WIP Mixing 354,000 / Cr Wages payable and MOH allocated 354,000; Dr WIP Aging 884,457 / Cr WIP Mixing 884,457.
case: Redwood Valley's Mixing supervisor estimates ending WIP is 25% converted. The plant manager, whose bonus depends on low cost per block transferred, suggests 'it's really more like 50%'. Use March data.
Recompute WA conversion EU and cost per EU at 50%.
What happens to the cost of blocks transferred out and to ending WIP?
Why might the plant manager prefer 50%?
How can the creamery make completion estimates more reliable?

CC EU 16,000 + 2,000 = 18,000; CC per EU 340,000 ÷ 18,000 = $18.89. Transferred out 16,000 × 48.689 = $779,022 (down $17,778); ending WIP rises to $156,978. Lower unit cost flatters the manager's performance. Use process timers, sensors and audits, and separate the estimator from the bonus.
exam: Explain equivalent units and why they're computed separately for materials and conversion costs.
EU = physical units × % complete; materials are often added at specific points while conversion is incurred evenly, so completion differs by category.

Beginning WIP 1,000 units (DM $9,000, CC $3,000); started 9,000; completed 8,000; ending 2,000 units (DM 100%, CC 50%). Current costs DM $91,000, CC $60,000. Using weighted average, compute costs transferred out and ending WIP.
outcomes: Compute WA cost per EU and assign costs
take: Average department costs over identical units

Units, EU, costs, cost per EU, assign
